beats.intro: Chapter four. [[sub]]Economies rise and fall in cycles. We look at how the cycle is felt in jobs and prices.
beats.cycle: [[a]]The economy does not grow in a straight line. Output cycles around its long-term trend. [[exp]]In an expansion, output, jobs and spending rise. [[peak]]At the peak, growth tops out. [[con]]In a contraction, they fall. A deep and lasting one is a recession. [[tr]]The trough is the bottom, and the cycle begins again.
beats.sectors: [[a]]Different parts of the economy swing by different amounts. [[c]]Among consumers, spending on durable goods, like cars, swings the most. Non-durables and services swing the least. [[inv]]Business investment swings even more than consumption. [[h]]Housing is very sensitive to interest rates and credit, and it often turns before the rest of the economy. [[t]]Trade depends on foreign growth and the exchange rate. Strong exports can offset weak domestic demand.
beats.unemp: [[a]]Here are a hundred working-age people. [[emp]]Sixty are employed. [[un]]Four are unemployed: they want work, and are looking. [[out]]The rest are outside the labor force. [[rate]]The unemployment rate is the unemployed divided by the labor force: four over sixty-four, about six point three percent. [[disc]]Now one unemployed person gets discouraged, and stops looking. [[after]]The labor force shrinks to sixty-three, unemployment to three, and the rate falls to four point eight percent, though nobody found a job. [[types]]Economists also separate frictional unemployment, between jobs; structural, from mismatched skills; and cyclical, from weak demand.
beats.infl: [[a]]Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. [[dis]]Disinflation means inflation is falling, but prices are still rising. [[def]]Deflation means the price level itself falls, so inflation is negative. [[hyp]]At the other extreme, hyperinflation: prices spiral upward out of control, and money loses its value.
beats.index: [[a]]How do we measure inflation? Price a fixed basket of goods. [[jan]]In January, fifty kilograms of rice at three, and seventy liters of gasoline at four point four, cost four hundred fifty-eight. [[feb]]In February, the same basket costs five hundred fifteen. [[idx]]Divide, and multiply by one hundred: the index is one twelve point four five. [[inf]]Inflation is the change in the index: twelve point four five percent. [[bias]]A fixed basket has biases. Shoppers switch to cheaper goods. Quality improves. New products are missing. All three push measured inflation upward.
beats.core: [[a]]Headline inflation uses every price in the basket. [[core]]Core inflation leaves out food and energy. [[spike]]When an oil price spike hits, headline jumps, but core barely moves. [[why]]Policy makers watch core, to avoid overreacting to swings that may not last.
beats.causes: [[a]]Economists describe two sources of inflation. [[cp]]Cost-push: rising costs, usually wages, push businesses to raise prices. [[dp]]Demand-pull: strong demand pulls prices up, and then workers ask for raises to catch up. [[root]]Either way, the root is demand running ahead of capacity. [[nairu]]When unemployment falls below its natural rate, called NAIRU, labor shortages appear, and wage pressure builds.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]The cycle runs from trough, through expansion to a peak, and then contraction. [[w2]]Unemployment rates can mislead, because discouraged workers leave the labor force. [[w3]]Price indexes track a fixed basket, with an upward bias; core inflation strips out food and energy. [[w4]]Inflation is cost-push or demand-pull, and it builds when unemployment falls below the natural rate.
